verdict: PASS — production evaluator meets the frozen gold benchmark

C1.whatIsNew: A reasonably sized (N=180), double-blind, sham-controlled RCT of a neuromodulation device found no benefit over sham on tinnitus distress at 12 weeks (between-group difference 1.4 THI points, p=0.43). The genuinely new information is a credible null result from a manufacturer-funded trial, which is notable because sponsor-funded device trials more often report positive findings.
C1.primaryEndpoint: Change in Tinnitus Handicap Inventory (THI) score at 12 weeks
C1.numericalResult: THI change: device −15.2 points, sham −13.8 points; between-group difference 1.4 points (95% CI −2.1 to 4.9), p=0.43
C1.loudnessEffect: none — no psychoacoustic loudness matching or loudness rating was reported, so this trial says nothing about the loudness of the tinnitus percept; THI change must not be read as a loudness effect.
C1.distressEffect: none — the device produced no distress benefit beyond sham (1.4-point THI difference, CI spanning zero); the large within-arm improvement in BOTH arms (−15.2 and −13.8) illustrates placebo/regression effects rather than device efficacy.
C1.clinicalSignificance: A 1.4-point THI difference is far below the commonly cited ~7-point minimal clinically important difference and the confidence interval excludes any clinically meaningful benefit, so patients would not notice a difference from this device versus sham.
C1.safetyObservations: Not reported — no adverse event data appear in the record provided
mainLimitations: Device 'X' is not identified in the record, so the result cannot yet be mapped to a specific treatment in the database
Only 12 weeks of follow-up; no longer-term or durability data
No psychoacoustic outcomes (loudness match, minimum masking level), so effects on the percept itself are untested
Adverse events and safety monitoring not reported in the available record
Manufacturer-funded with two employee authors; trial registration/pre-specification and analysis plan not verifiable from the record
No reported subgroup or responder analyses, so a benefit in a narrower phenotype cannot be excluded or claimed
Single trial, no independent replication
C1.conflictOfInterest: manufacturer-funded / author equity — funded by the device manufacturer and two authors are company employees; notably the sponsored trial reported a null result, which reduces concern about outcome-favourable bias here, though sponsor control of design and reporting remains a limitation
C1.weeklyTitle: Neuromodulation device performs no better than sham in 180-person tinnitus trial
C1.whyMatters: Both the real device and a fake (sham) version produced similar improvements in tinnitus distress, meaning the improvement came from expectation and time rather than the device itself. This is a useful reminder that uncontrolled 'before and after' improvements in tinnitus studies can be misleading.
C1.factuallyVerifiedReason: Primary source: peer-reviewed publication in an otology journal with an available PMID, reporting a pre-specified between-group comparison with effect size, CI and p-value. The specific PMID and the device identity should be recorded before publication, but the factual claim itself is adequately sourced.
C1.summaryForAdmin: Well-designed, double-blind, sham-controlled RCT (N=180) showing no benefit of a manufacturer's neuromodulation device over sham on THI at 12 weeks (1.4 points, p=0.43); both arms improved ~14-15 points, a textbook placebo/regression pattern. No loudness or psychoacoustic outcomes, so no loudness conclusion is possible; safety data not reported. Flagged major only because the identity of 'device X' needs resolving — if it maps to a device already scored in the database, this negative sham-controlled trial should lower that treatment's evidence score and be used as a cautionary reference for within-group-only claims.

C2.whatIsNew: A newly reported independent randomized placebo-controlled trial of oral drug Y (N=90) in chronic tinnitus that missed its pre-specified primary endpoint (TFI change at week 8, p=0.21); the only positive finding is a post-hoc subgroup loudness VAS result in participants with high-frequency hearing loss.
C2.population: Adults with chronic tinnitus; a subset had high-frequency hearing loss (subgroup size not reported)
C2.primaryEndpoint: Change in Tinnitus Functional Index (TFI) at week 8
C2.secondaryEndpoints: Loudness VAS (reported as significant only in a post-hoc subgroup with high-frequency hearing loss); other secondary endpoints not reported
C2.numericalResult: Primary TFI change at week 8: p=0.21 (not significant). Secondary loudness VAS in post-hoc high-frequency hearing loss subgroup: p=0.03. No effect sizes, means, or confidence intervals reported.
C2.loudnessEffect: limited — the only loudness signal is a post-hoc subgroup VAS result (p=0.03) with no effect size reported, which is hypothesis-generating at best and cannot be treated as evidence that the drug reduces the tinnitus percept.
C2.distressEffect: none — the pre-specified distress endpoint (TFI at week 8) did not separate from placebo (p=0.21).
C2.clinicalSignificance: No demonstrated clinical benefit: the trial failed on its pre-specified distress endpoint, and the subgroup loudness p-value comes with no effect size, so nothing here shows a change patients would notice.
mainLimitations: Pre-specified primary endpoint (TFI at week 8) was negative
The positive loudness finding is post-hoc and restricted to a subgroup, with no multiplicity correction described
Subgroup size not reported; likely underpowered and prone to false positives
No effect sizes or confidence intervals reported, only p-values
Modest total sample (N=90) for detecting realistic tinnitus treatment effects
Short 8-week endpoint; no longer-term follow-up reported
Blinding procedures and adverse-event data not described
Single trial, no independent replication of the subgroup signal
C2.conflictOfInterest: independent — described as independent academic funding; no manufacturer sponsorship or author equity disclosed in the record provided.
C2.weeklyTitle: Oral drug Y fails its main endpoint in a 90-person placebo-controlled tinnitus trial
C2.whyMatters: This independently funded trial found no benefit of drug Y on tinnitus distress compared with placebo after 8 weeks. A loudness improvement appeared only in an after-the-fact analysis of one subgroup, which is the kind of finding that often disappears when tested properly, so it should not be read as evidence the drug works.
C2.factuallyVerifiedReason: Peer-reviewed publication with a PMID and a clearly described pre-specified primary endpoint and result; the factual report is verifiable as a primary source, though the underlying subgroup analysis is exploratory.
C2.summaryForAdmin: Negative RCT: oral drug Y missed its pre-specified TFI primary endpoint at week 8 (p=0.21) in 90 chronic tinnitus patients, with independent academic funding and a PMID. The only positive result is a post-hoc subgroup loudness VAS (p=0.03, no effect size, subgroup size unreported), which is hypothesis-generating and must not be presented as a loudness benefit. Publish as a negative result; no score or rank change, and drug Y should not be added as a supported treatment on this basis.

C3.whatIsNew: A university clinic reports that 45 people completed a new 10-week sound therapy program with a mean 18-point improvement on the THI. What is new is the specific program, not any demonstration that it works — there was no control group, so the change cannot be attributed to the therapy.
C3.population: Tinnitus patients attending a university clinic; further demographic, duration and hearing-loss details Not reported
C3.primaryEndpoint: Change in Tinnitus Handicap Inventory (THI) from baseline to 10 weeks
C3.comparisonType: within-group only — NEVER present within-group improvement as proof of efficacy
C3.numericalResult: Mean THI improvement of 18 points from baseline at 10 weeks, p<0.001 (single-arm, no comparator)
C3.loudnessEffect: none — no psychoacoustic loudness matching or loudness rating was reported, and THI change says nothing about the loudness of the percept.
C3.distressEffect: limited — an 18-point within-group THI drop is consistent with a distress benefit, but with no control arm it cannot be separated from placebo response, regression to the mean, natural fluctuation and repeated-assessment effects, all of which routinely produce 10–15 point THI changes in uncontrolled tinnitus cohorts.
C3.otherOutcomes: Not reported (no sleep, quality-of-life, anxiety or audiometric outcomes described)
C3.clinicalSignificance: The magnitude exceeds the usual ~7-point THI minimal clinically important difference, so if it were causal it would matter to patients — but the uncontrolled design means the attributable effect of the program is unknown.
C3.safetyObservations: Not reported — no adverse events, dropouts or tolerability data described
mainLimitations: No control or sham arm; improvement cannot be attributed to the intervention
Not randomized, not blinded, open-label — high expectation/placebo susceptibility
Small sample (N=45), single centre
Only 10 weeks; no follow-up to test durability
THI measures distress/handicap only; no loudness or psychoacoustic measures
Dropouts, adverse events and per-protocol vs intention-to-treat analysis not reported
Authors' conclusion that the program 'is effective' is not supported by the design
C3.conflictOfInterest: unclear — university clinic with no industry funding disclosed; absence of a disclosure statement is not the same as confirmed independence, and no author COI statement is described
C3.weeklyTitle: Uncontrolled 45-person study of a new sound therapy program reports lower tinnitus distress scores
C3.whyMatters: People in this small study reported feeling considerably less bothered by their tinnitus after 10 weeks, but because everyone received the therapy and there was no comparison group, we cannot tell how much of that came from the program itself rather than time, attention and expectation. Nothing here measures whether the tinnitus sound itself got quieter.
C3.factuallyVerifiedReason: The primary record supplies the design, sample size, duration, endpoint and effect size, so the factual claim ('an uncontrolled 45-patient study reported an 18-point mean THI improvement') can be reported accurately. It may only be published with explicit 'single-arm, no control group' framing and must not repeat the authors' efficacy conclusion; a journal/registry citation should be attached before publication since none was supplied.
C3.summaryForAdmin: Open-label single-arm study (N=45) of a new sound therapy program showing an 18-point within-group THI improvement at 10 weeks. The design cannot support the authors' claim of effectiveness — no control, no randomization, no blinding, no follow-up, and THI is a distress measure with no loudness data at all. Archive as a hypothesis-generating pilot; no score or rank change, and it should not be used to support any loudness claim.

C4.whatIsNew: Nothing new that can be assessed: a content-free conference abstract claiming 'promise' for an unspecified neuromodulation approach, with no design, sample size, or numbers. The only new information is that some group is presenting unpublished neuromodulation work.
C4.population: Not reported ('tinnitus patients', no further detail)
C4.comparisonType: Not reported — NEVER present within-group improvement as proof of efficacy
C4.loudnessEffect: none — the abstract reports no psychoacoustic loudness matching or loudness ratings at all, and 'meaningful improvements' cannot be read as a change in the percept.
C4.distressEffect: none — no THI/TFI/TQ or other distress instrument, score, or effect size is reported; 'meaningful improvements' is uninterpretable.
C4.clinicalSignificance: Impossible to judge: with no effect size, no comparator, and no outcome instrument named, nothing here tells a patient whether anything would change for them.
C4.safetyObservations: Not reported — the abstract makes no statement about adverse events, tolerability, or dropouts.
mainLimitations: Conference abstract only; no peer-reviewed full paper
No sample size reported
No study design reported (randomization, control, blinding all unknown)
No numerical results or effect sizes
No named outcome measures — cannot separate loudness from distress
No trial registration number located, so pre-specified endpoints cannot be checked
Unknown funding and conflicts of interest
'Neuromodulation approach' is unspecified — cannot be mapped to an existing treatment record
No follow-up duration reported
C4.conflictOfInterest: unclear — no funding statement, sponsor, or author disclosure available in the abstract; manufacturer involvement can neither be confirmed nor excluded.
C4.weeklyTitle: Conference abstract reports unspecified neuromodulation results in tinnitus, with no data released
C4.whyMatters: A conference presentation says a neuromodulation treatment 'showed promise' for tinnitus, but no numbers, patient counts, or study design have been published, so there is nothing to evaluate. Claims like this should be treated as a placeholder until a full paper or trial registration appears.
C4.factuallyVerifiedReason: The abstract contains no verifiable factual content — no sample size, design, outcome measures, numbers, or registration number — and no primary source exists to confirm even the basic claim. Reporting it would amount to republishing an unsupported promotional statement.
C4.summaryForAdmin: Empty-shell conference abstract: 'neuromodulation shows promise' with zero design details, zero numbers, and no registry entry. It supports no loudness or distress conclusion and must not move any score, tier, or ranking; the vague phrase 'meaningful improvements' is exactly the kind of wording that gets mistaken for a loudness effect. Recommend park it on a watch list and revisit only if a full paper or registration appears.

C5.whatIsNew: A double-blind, sham-controlled RCT (N=120, 8 weeks) of wearable device Z reports a between-group THI advantage of about 7 points over sham (active −11 vs sham −4, p=0.01). What is new is the sham-controlled distress signal for this device; nothing new is shown about the tinnitus percept itself, since no psychoacoustic measurements were made.
C5.population: Adults with tinnitus enrolled in a randomized sham-controlled device trial; further demographic, etiology, duration and severity details Not reported
C5.primaryEndpoint: Tinnitus Handicap Inventory (THI) change at 8 weeks (as reported; formal primary endpoint designation Not reported)
C5.numericalResult: THI: active −11 points vs sham −4 points; between-group p=0.01 (between-group difference ≈7 points). No psychoacoustic loudness data.
C5.loudnessEffect: none — no psychoacoustic loudness matching or loudness rating was performed, so this trial says nothing about whether the tinnitus percept itself got quieter; the abstract's phrase 'tinnitus was significantly reduced' overstates a distress-questionnaire result.
C5.distressEffect: moderate — a genuine sham-controlled between-group reduction in tinnitus handicap of roughly 7 THI points at 8 weeks, which is a real but modest distress effect.
C5.clinicalSignificance: A ~7-point between-group THI difference sits right at the commonly cited minimal clinically important difference (about 7 points), so the average patient benefit is borderline-perceptible rather than clearly meaningful, and it concerns distress/handicap only.
C5.safetyObservations: Not reported — the record contains no adverse-event data for the 120 participants over 8 weeks.
mainLimitations: No psychoacoustic measurement of loudness or any percept-level outcome; abstract wording ('tinnitus was significantly reduced') conflates distress with the percept
Between-group THI difference (~7 points) is only at/near the MCID threshold
Short 8-week treatment period with no reported longer-term follow-up or durability data
Industry-sponsored, single trial, no independent replication
No safety/adverse-event reporting in the record
Blinding integrity of a wearable sham not verified (no blinding-success check reported)
Population characteristics, responder rates, and secondary endpoints not reported
C5.conflictOfInterest: manufacturer-funded — industry-sponsored trial of the sponsor's own device; individual author equity, employment or consulting relationships not specified in the record and should be checked in the published disclosure statement.
C5.weeklyTitle: Sham-controlled trial of wearable device Z: modest improvement in tinnitus distress questionnaire, no loudness measured
C5.whyMatters: In a properly blinded trial with a dummy device, people using device Z reported somewhat less tinnitus-related distress than those using the sham, but the difference was small and only just at the level patients typically notice. The study did not measure whether the sound itself became quieter, so claims that 'tinnitus was reduced' should be read as 'tinnitus bother was reduced'.
C5.factuallyVerifiedReason: The item is a registered, peer-reviewed randomized sham-controlled trial with reported between-group numbers, which is sufficient to report factually; the reporting must, however, correct the abstract's conflation of distress with the tinnitus percept and disclose the industry sponsorship.
C5.summaryForAdmin: Reasonably designed double-blind sham-controlled RCT (N=120, 8 weeks) showing a ~7-point between-group THI advantage for wearable device Z — a distress-only result, since no psychoacoustic measurements were taken; the authors' 'tinnitus was significantly reduced' claim must not be published as a loudness effect. Effect size is borderline against the THI MCID, the trial is manufacturer-funded, unreplicated, short-term, and reports no safety data. Flagged major only to hold for deeper review of any distress-rating change; no score or rank change is proposed on this single sponsored trial.

C6.whatIsNew: First public safety report of three first-time seizures occurring within hours of use of consumer neurostimulation device Q for tinnitus, now acknowledged by the national regulator as under evaluation. This is a new safety signal, not efficacy data.
C6.population: Three patients using consumer neurostimulation device Q for tinnitus; demographics, seizure history and concomitant medications not reported
C6.primaryEndpoint: Not reported — uncontrolled adverse-event case series plus regulator safety communication
C6.numericalResult: 3 first-time seizures reported within hours of device use; no denominator of exposed users, no incidence rate, no background-rate comparison reported
C6.loudnessEffect: none — no psychoacoustic loudness matching or loudness ratings were reported; this item concerns harm, not the tinnitus percept.
C6.distressEffect: none — no THI/TFI/TQ, anxiety, sleep or QoL outcomes were reported.
C6.clinicalSignificance: Seizures are a serious, potentially life-changing harm, so even three temporally close cases matter to patients considering this device — but causality is unestablished and no exposure denominator exists.
C6.safetyObservations: Three first-time seizures reported within hours of using consumer neurostimulation device Q; regulator states it 'is aware of the reports and is evaluating'. No information on prior seizure risk factors, device settings, concomitant drugs, or total user exposure.
mainLimitations: Case series of only 3 patients with no control group and no comparison to background seizure incidence
No exposure denominator, so no rate can be calculated
Temporal association does not establish causation; confounders (sleep deprivation, alcohol, medication, undiagnosed epilepsy) not reported
Regulator has only acknowledged receipt of reports — no completed assessment, no finding, no regulatory action
Voluntary adverse-event reporting is subject to reporting and publicity bias
Device parameters, usage pattern and whether use was on-label are not described
C6.conflictOfInterest: unclear — funding and reporter affiliations not stated; no manufacturer involvement disclosed in the safety communication
C6.weeklyTitle: Regulator evaluating reports of three first-time seizures after use of a consumer neurostimulation device for tinnitus
C6.whyMatters: Three people reportedly had their first-ever seizure within hours of using a consumer nerve-stimulation device for tinnitus, and the national regulator says it is looking into it. Three cases cannot prove the device caused the seizures, but it is a serious enough possibility that anyone using or considering such a device should know about it.
C6.factuallyVerifiedReason: The existence of the reports and the regulator's 'aware and evaluating' status are documented on an official regulator safety-communication page, which is an authoritative primary source for that fact. What is NOT verified is causality or any regulatory conclusion, so the item may only be reported as unconfirmed adverse-event reports under review.
C6.summaryForAdmin: Uncontrolled 3-patient adverse-event series plus an official regulator notice reporting first-time seizures hours after use of consumer neurostimulation device Q for tinnitus; the regulator has only acknowledged receipt and is still evaluating. No efficacy, loudness or distress data, no denominator, and no causal determination — so no efficacy score should move, but this warrants a visible safety flag on the device entry and a watch on the regulator page for a formal finding. Flagged major so the safety assessment (not the evidence score) gets human review before publication.

C7.whatIsNew: A company press release claims a pivotal trial of treatment W 'met its endpoints' and anticipates FDA approval, but no data, no publication, and no posted registry results accompany the claim.
C7.primaryEndpoint: Not reported — 'endpoints' asserted as met but never specified
C7.comparisonType: Not reported — NEVER present within-group improvement as proof of efficacy
C7.loudnessEffect: none — no psychoacoustic loudness matching or percept-loudness data of any kind is presented, and nothing in the release permits any inference about the tinnitus percept.
C7.distressEffect: none — no THI/TFI/TQ or other validated distress instrument results are reported; the unspecified 'endpoints' could be distress, loudness, or something else entirely.
C7.clinicalSignificance: Unable to assess: with no effect sizes, no comparator, and no endpoint definition, there is no basis to judge whether anything meaningful happened for patients.
C7.safetyObservations: Not reported — the release makes no statement about adverse events, dropouts, or tolerability.
mainLimitations: No data tables, no effect sizes, no confidence intervals
No peer-reviewed publication
No registry results posted; trial registration not verifiable from the release
Primary endpoint not specified — cannot tell whether it was loudness, distress, or another measure
Sample size, population, randomization, blinding and control condition all unstated
Claim of FDA approval 'next year' is a company expectation, not a regulatory record
'Standard of care' framing is marketing language, not evidence
Self-reported by the party with financial interest in the result
C7.conflictOfInterest: manufacturer-funded — the sponsor is the sole source, has direct commercial interest in the claim, and no independent verification exists; author/investigator conflicts cannot be assessed because no authors are named.
C7.weeklyTitle: Company reports its pivotal tinnitus trial met endpoints; no data or publication released
C7.whyMatters: A company says its tinnitus treatment succeeded in a pivotal trial, but has not released any numbers, published a paper, or posted trial results, so there is nothing yet to check. Until the actual data appear, this is an announcement rather than evidence, and it should not change how anyone rates the treatment.
C7.factuallyVerifiedReason: The only verifiable fact is that the company made the statement; the underlying trial claims cannot be confirmed against any paper, registry entry, or regulatory record. It may be published in the weekly feed only as a clearly labeled company-reported development, with the absence of data stated explicitly.
C7.summaryForAdmin: Unverified sponsor press release asserting a pivotal trial 'met its endpoints' for treatment W, with zero supporting data, no publication, and no registry results. It supports no loudness or distress rating whatsoever — the endpoints are not even specified — and the FDA approval expectation is a company forecast, not a regulatory record. Log as a watch item on treatment W and re-review when a paper or ClinicalTrials.gov results posting appears; no score or rank change.

C8.whatIsNew: A university lab reports that compound R abolished behavioral evidence of tinnitus in a mouse noise-exposure model (n=12 per group). It is a new preclinical candidate signal only — no human data of any kind.
C8.population: Noise-exposed mice (animal model of tinnitus); no humans
C8.primaryEndpoint: Behavioral evidence of tinnitus in treated vs control animals (behavioral assay not specified in the record, e.g. gap-prepulse inhibition-type paradigm)
C8.numericalResult: none reported — described qualitatively as 'eliminated behavioral evidence of tinnitus' in treated animals vs controls; no effect sizes, test statistics or confidence intervals given in the record
C8.loudnessEffect: none — animal behavioral proxies cannot measure the human tinnitus percept, and no psychoacoustic loudness matching exists here; any claim about loudness reduction would be unsupported.
C8.distressEffect: none — no THI/TFI/TQ, anxiety, sleep or quality-of-life measures are possible in this design.
C8.clinicalSignificance: No clinical significance can be assigned: mouse behavioral readouts have historically translated poorly to human tinnitus, and no patient-relevant outcome was measured.
C8.safetyObservations: Not reported — no toxicity, tolerability or adverse-event data described for compound R in this record.
mainLimitations: Animal model only; no human data
Very small groups (n=12 per group)
Behavioral tinnitus assays in rodents are indirect proxies with known false-positive/negative issues (e.g. gap-detection confounds from hearing loss or hyperacusis)
Randomization and blinding of assessors not reported
No numerical results, effect sizes or variance reported in the record
No dose-response, pharmacokinetic, or safety/toxicology data reported
No independent replication
Absence of behavioral evidence is not equivalent to elimination of a percept
C8.conflictOfInterest: unclear — described as a university lab with no funding or disclosure information provided; no manufacturer sponsorship stated but none explicitly ruled out
C8.weeklyTitle: Experimental compound removes tinnitus-like behavior in mice; no human evidence yet
C8.whyMatters: In a small laboratory study, mice exposed to loud noise stopped showing behavior that suggests tinnitus after being given an experimental compound. This is a very early lab finding in animals — it does not tell us whether the compound would reduce tinnitus loudness or distress in people, and most such findings never make it to a working human treatment.
C8.factuallyVerifiedReason: The item is a primary peer-reviewed preclinical report rather than a press release, so the factual claim (a mouse study with this result) can be reported as such; however, no citation, DOI or numerical data were supplied, so the specific figures cannot be independently checked and should not be quoted.
C8.summaryForAdmin: Preclinical mouse study of compound R with n=12/group, reporting elimination of tinnitus-like behavior; no numbers, no blinding/randomization details, no safety data, no human data. This is candidate-pipeline intelligence at best and should not affect any treatment score, tier or loudness/distress rating. File as an early new-treatment-candidate to watch for a first-in-human or registry entry.
